summaries.example: Imagine a science book using numbers to describe how fast a toy car moves. A platonist may say numbers really exist, even though we cannot see them. A nominalist may say the book can use numbers successfully without numbers existing as separate, invisible things. The disagreement is about what mathematics talks about, not about whether counting and measuring are useful.
summaries.summary: Nominalism about mathematics is the idea that numbers, sets, and other mathematical objects do not exist as separate abstract things, or that we do not need to assume that they exist. Platonism takes the opposite position: mathematical objects exist, although they are not physical objects that we can find in space and time. The disagreement matters because mathematics is used successfully in science. A nominalist needs to explain how mathematics can help scientists without mathematical objects being part of reality. The entry describes several possible answers. Mathematical fictionalism treats mathematics somewhat like a useful story and says it can help shorten scientific reasoning. Modal structuralism talks about possible structures instead of actual mathematical objects. Deflationary nominalism keeps ordinary mathematical statements and argues that saying “there are numbers” need not make us committed to numbers existing. The entry examines how these views handle knowledge, scientific use, language, and their basic ideas about what exists.
key_ideas: Nominalists and platonists disagree about whether numbers and other mathematical things exist.
Mathematics works very well in science, so nominalists must explain why it is useful without relying on mathematical objects.
Some nominalists rewrite scientific or mathematical ideas; others keep the usual language and explain why it does not require commitment to numbers.
The entry compares three approaches: fictionalism, modal structuralism, and deflationary nominalism.
Each approach solves some problems but faces questions of its own.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate asks a basic question: what are we talking about when we do mathematics? It also connects mathematics with science. Understanding the different answers helps us see that a tool can be useful even when philosophers disagree about what the tool’s words describe. It shows why a simple question about numbers can lead to larger questions about truth, knowledge, language, and reality.

important_terms.definition: The view that mathematical objects, such as numbers, do not exist, or do not need to exist for mathematics to make sense.
The view that mathematical objects exist, even though they are not physical objects in space and time.
A thing that is not in a place or time and does not cause physical events, such as a mathematical object is said to be.
The idea that mathematics is needed in our best scientific explanations, such as explanations using numbers and equations.
A careful argument or translation that tries to explain mathematics without saying that mathematical objects exist.

questions_to_think_about: Can a story be useful even if the things in it are not real?
When scientists use numbers, must they believe that numbers exist?
Is using a word the same as saying the thing named by the word exists?

summaries.example: Suppose a physicist uses an equation involving functions and sets to predict a laboratory result. A platonist can treat the equation literally: it refers to abstract mathematical entities, and those entities help make the theory true. A nominalist must explain the prediction without commitment to such entities. A fictionalist might reformulate the physical theory in nominalistic terms and argue that mathematics is conservative: added mathematics helps organize derivations without producing new conclusions about the physical world. A deflationary nominalist instead keeps the equation and denies that quantifying over mathematical objects automatically commits us to their existence.
summaries.summary:
The entry surveys mathematical nominalism, the family of views that reject or minimize commitment to abstract mathematical objects. It contrasts nominalism with platonism, according to which numbers, sets, relations, and structures exist abstractly. The central pressure on platonism is epistemological: abstract objects seem unable to cause our beliefs, so it is difficult to explain mathematical knowledge. The central pressure on nominalism concerns application: mathematics is deeply involved in successful science, and nominalists must explain that success without treating mathematical entities as real. Other issues include whether mathematics and science can receive a uniform semantics, whether mathematical claims can be interpreted literally, and what entities a theory is ultimately committed to.

The entry examines three nominalist programs. Fictionalism rejects the truth of unqualified existential mathematical claims but adds a fiction-like operator, such as “according to arithmetic.” It explains usefulness through conservativeness and attempts to reformulate scientific theories without mathematical objects, though questions remain about metalogic, set theory, and actual scientific practice. Modal structuralism replaces talk of mathematical objects with claims about possible structures. This avoids some ontological commitments but raises questions about how structural possibility is known and how mathematics is first applied to the physical world. Deflationary nominalism accepts that mathematics may be indispensable and that mathematical statements may be true, while denying that quantification alone establishes existence. Its relatively modest reconstruction is an advantage, but its account of existence and reference remains controversial. The overall assessment is—
key_ideas: Platonism has an epistemological challenge: if mathematical objects are abstract and causally disconnected from us, how do we know mathematical truths?
Nominalism has a major application challenge: if mathematics refers to nothing, how does it contribute to successful science?
Platonism can preserve ordinary mathematical syntax and a broadly uniform semantics for mathematics and science; nominalist reconstructions may alter one or both.
Fictionalism and modal structuralism take demanding routes by reformulating theories, while deflationary nominalism rejects the inference from quantifier commitment to ontological commitment.
The entry treats these as competing strategies with partial successes, not as a settled dispute.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters because it tests what mathematical language and scientific explanation commit us to. If mathematics is indispensable to science, one might think mathematical objects must exist. But the entry shows that this inference depends on a particular account of ontological commitment. The debate therefore links philosophy of mathematics to epistemology, metaphysics, philosophy of language, and philosophy of science. It also clarifies the difference between explaining why mathematics is useful, explaining how scientists actually use it, and deciding what mathematical claims mean.

important_terms.definition: A position holding that mathematical objects, relations, or structures do not exist, or need not be accepted as abstract entities in order to understand mathematics.
The position that mathematical objects and structures exist as abstract entities, outside space-time and without causal powers.
The question of what entities a theory commits us to. The entry distinguishes quantifying over something from being committed to its existence.
The claim that mathematical entities are needed in our best scientific theories, often used to argue for belief in those entities.
A property of a mathematical theory such that, when added to suitable non-mathematical claims, it yields no new conclusions about the physical world that were unavailable without it.
A nominalist strategy that treats mathematical discourse as useful fiction and often introduces phrases such as “according to arithmetic.”
A view that interprets mathematics through possible structures rather than existing mathematical objects.

A view that separates existential quantification from ontological commitment, allowing mathematical statements to be true without numbers existing independently of linguistic or psychological practices.

questions_to_think_about: Does the successful use of mathematics support the existence of mathematical objects, or only the usefulness of mathematical descriptions?
Can a theory be true while its quantifiers do not carry ontological commitment?
Does translating ordinary mathematics into modal or fictional language preserve what mathematicians actually mean?
If mathematics is conservative, why can it make scientific reasoning shorter or easier?
What kind of evidence would establish that a mathematical structure is genuinely possible?

summaries.example: Your class uses a graph to show how a plant grows. The graph has points and numbers, but the plant is a physical thing. A platonist might say the numbers and mathematical patterns used in the graph exist as abstract objects. A nominalist might say the graph is a useful way to describe the plant without assuming that numbers exist independently. Some nominalists would replace the graph’s mathematical language with descriptions of comparisons, such as which plant is taller or which change is greater. Others would keep the graph and argue that using “there are five measurements” does not automatically commit us to abstract numbers.
summaries.summary:
The philosophy of mathematics includes a dispute between platonism and nominalism. Platonists say that numbers, sets, and mathematical structures exist as abstract objects. They are not physical objects, but they are still supposed to be real. Nominalists deny that these objects exist, or say that mathematics can be understood without taking them to exist. Because mathematics is used throughout science, nominalists need to explain why it is so successful. This is often called the application problem.

The entry also discusses a problem for platonism: if mathematical objects are outside space and time and cannot cause events, how do humans gain knowledge about them? Nominalists avoid that particular puzzle, but they face other questions. Can they explain the difference between someone who understands advanced mathematics and someone who does not? Can they describe scientific practice without rewriting mathematics? Can they use the same meaning for mathematical and scientific statements?

Three approaches receive special attention. Fictionalism treats mathematical language as useful in a way similar to a story or make-believe framework. Modal structuralism talks about possible structures rather than actual mathematical objects. Deflationary nominalism keeps much of ordinary mathematical language and separates being counted by a theory from really existing. Each approach addresses important concerns, but each also leaves philosophical problems for further discussion.
key_ideas: Platonism and nominalism offer different answers to the question of what mathematics is about.
Platonism faces the puzzle of how people gain knowledge of abstract objects.
Nominalism faces the puzzle of how mathematics can work so well in science if mathematical objects are not real.
Changing mathematical language may help nominalism avoid abstract objects, but it may also make the language less like the mathematics people actually use.
Deflationary nominalism says that saying “there are” some things in a theory does not by itself prove that those things exist independently.
The entry compares several forms of nominalism rather than presenting nominalism as one single theory.
summaries.why_it_matters: Numbers and equations are not just found in mathematics classes. They are used in science to model motion, growth, probability, and many other things. This debate asks whether that use tells us what numbers really are. It also teaches an important philosophical lesson: a theory can be useful, understandable, and successful while people still disagree about what its language commits us to. Studying the disagreement helps us examine assumptions that usually remain hidden.

important_terms.definition: The view that numbers and other mathematical objects do not exist, or do not have to be assumed to exist.
The view that mathematical objects exist as abstract, nonphysical objects.
An abstract thing is not located in space or time and does not cause physical events.
A reason for believing in something because it is necessary for our best explanations, especially scientific explanations.
The philosophical question of how we can know mathematical truths, especially if mathematical objects are abstract.
The challenge of explaining why mathematics helps us describe and predict events in the physical world.
A view that treats mathematical statements as useful within a kind of story or framework, without saying that mathematical objects exist.
A view that explains mathematics using possible patterns or structures instead of existing mathematical objects.

questions_to_think_about: If a map helps you travel, must every feature on the map exist in the same way as roads and buildings?
Does using a number mean that you believe the number exists?
Would changing the language of science change the science itself?
Is it easier to explain mathematical knowledge or the success of mathematics in science?
Which view seems to preserve ordinary mathematical talk best?
